floor_history.headline: mk_g2l floor 17 -> 7: holding the 0x86 compare value in the dead a0 param fixes four register families at once; residual is one pseudo that inherits $a0's hard-reg preference via global.c expand_prefe

frontier.hypothesis: The compare-value holder need not be the a0 PARAMETER — any single variable serving both the 0x86 compare and the call's first argument should give the same allocation, which would retire the parameter-reuse policy question entirely.
frontier.mechanism: The cascade needs one pseudo carrying both roles so it takes $a0 via the call-arg copy preference; nothing in expand_preferences/allocno_compare cares that the pseudo began as an incoming parameter.
frontier.next_probe: Declare 's32 id;' (the value passed as func_80032854's first arg), use it for the 0x86 compare AND for every '*(s16 *)(obj + 4)' assignment, pass id; sandbox --disable all. Same 7 => switch the candidate to that spelling. Worse => the parameter identity is load-bearing and the reuse needs carve-out treatment (Judge/owner call, not self-approval).

frontier.hypothesis: Blocking the expand_preferences merge that hands $a0/$a1 to the call-path obj pseudo makes it fall back to the alloc-order first-free register $v0 — target — closing 5 of the 7 residual diffs.
frontier.mechanism: global.c:797-840 skips the merge when the two allocnos conflict (CONFLICTP either direction) or when there is no REG_DEAD note. Note the conflict matrix lists each allocno as conflicting with ITSELF, so a single_set of the shape 'x = *(s16 *)(x + 4)' is skipped outright.
frontier.next_probe: Enumerate pure-C forms where (a) the arg/compare value is live at the point a call-path obj is loaded, or (b) the obj variable is also the arg variable on some paths, and after each form read ';; 78 preferences:' out of base.i.greg — the dump reports whether the merge was blocked immediately, without waiting for the score to move.

frontier.hypothesis: The 2-diff stack-param load order is a scheduling-priority artifact: arg_a2 is consumed at the jal (longest path to exit) so priority scheduling should emit its load FIRST, which is what target does; our v1-first order is the anomaly.
frontier.mechanism: Both loads sit in the entry block, so emission order is the scheduler's INSN_PRIORITY / LUID ordering.
frontier.next_probe: Read the two loads' INSN_PRIORITY in tmp/grind/mk_g2l/s1/base.i.sched, then measure the two single-alias variants separately (keep arg_a2, test stack_v1 directly; and vice-versa) — K2 dropped BOTH aliases at once and only the combined drop is known to be worse.
